title: Chapter 153 – The Road Pebble Knows
html:
[The Silver Road – Lin Jian]

The road begins at the old house, at the foot of the stone step where he sat as a child, and for the first mile it looks like nothing at all.

Jian stands on the step in the gray hour before sunrise with a pack on his back and a staff in his hand, and looks at the packed earth of the yard. It is the same yard. There is the well. There is the crooked apple tree, the first grafted daughter of the Mother Tree, and the line of washing, and the kitchen door with its patch of lamp-light. The whole Garden is asleep except for a few. Behind him on the porch Qinghe stands with her arms folded and her chin high, and Zhao with the baby, and Feng with his head tilted, and a little apart, on the lowest step, Tian Mo, leaning on his staff. Nobody has made a speech. They said their goodbyes in the night, over the last bowl of soup. What is left is only this: the cold, and the people who love him, and the nine paces of frozen mud between where he stands and the place where the road begins.

Qinghe comes down the steps at the last moment and presses a lidded clay pot into his hands.

"It is rice and pickled radish," she says. "It will keep for three days. After that you may eat what you find, but you will eat it with the knowledge that I am disappointed."

"Mother."

"Do not mother me." Her chin trembles once, and firms. "Go on. Take your road."

Feng limps up behind her with a blanket over his shoulders, head cocked. He does not speak at first. He only puts out a thin dry hand and grips Jian's elbow. When he does speak it is in a whisper, so low that Jian has to bend to hear.

"The Wall knocks at night," he says. "Not like the Gate. Slower. Heavier. I have not told them. I do not want to frighten the children."

"Feng—"

"I just wanted you to hear it from me." The old man's eyes are unfocused and kind. "It is probably nothing. Go and fetch your seven. Come back before it is something."

Jian nods. He cannot trust his voice. He kisses his mother's forehead, and Feng's gray cheek, and turns, and goes down the three steps of the old house for the last time.

Can you see it? asks the boy.

Not yet.

Pebble says wait for the light.

He waits. Beside him Yue stands with her hands folded in her sleeves, in a plain quilted cloak, with Pebble on her shoulder. Bell has already shouldered her satchel, a bundle the size of a small horse, and is checking the knots with a doctor's absorbed frown. They are a strange party. An old white-haired man, a deaf woman who hears the earth, a clinician, a stone with a crack down its back, and a child who exists only in the corner of an old man's mind. He had imagined, once, that when he finally went to the sixth door it would be at the head of an army.

The sun comes over the ridge.

It does not rise gently. It strikes the top of Cloud Peak and the dome of the observatory flares white, and a single beam of light comes down out of it, thin as a thread and perfectly straight, across the valley and the orchard and the roof of the old house, and touches the earth at his feet.

And the road is there.

It is not a road. It is a line, a hand's breadth wide, of silver light lying along the ground, faintly humming. It runs north from the step across the yard and the wall and the frozen fields and away into the hills, as straight as a ruled stroke, and where it passes over the grass the frost is melted in a clean narrow ribbon.

"There," says Pebble.

* * *

They walk it for four hours before anyone says a word.

It is hard walking. The light does not bear weight, but it hums, a deep faint note that Yue hears with her whole body and Jian feels in his teeth, and stepping off it brings a cold that seeps up through the boots. So they keep to it, in single file: Pebble first, trotting along the silver on his four short legs with his tail up; then Yue; then Bell, swearing quietly at her satchel; then Jian, with his staff. The frost-white hills roll away on either side. Far behind, the Garden has dwindled to a smudge of smoke.

At noon the road climbs over a ridge and the world opens. Jian stops. He has never been this far north. Below them lies a long wide valley, brown and bare, with a frozen river meandering down the middle, and beyond it, filling half the sky, a wall of blue-white mountains so tall and so distant that they look painted on the air.

"The Sky Wall," says Bell, behind him. She has stopped too, breathing hard. "I have only seen it on Ning's chart."

"It looks closer than it is."

"It looks like it is leaning."

He looks again, and sees what she means. The peaks are very still, but the snow along their upper edges has a ragged, crumbling look, as if the whole range had been shaken once and set down badly. A thin gray haze hangs along the foot of them, and in the clear cold air he can see it move.

Dust, says the boy.

Perhaps.

Or breath.

He says nothing. He lifts his staff and walks on.

* * *

The silver road, it turns out, has rules.

He learns the first of them that afternoon, when a gap opens in front of him. It happens where the path crosses a stream, a shallow brown thing with ice at the edges. The light runs straight over the water, as it ran over the frost, and Pebble trots across it without a pause. Yue follows. Bell wades through, with her skirts hitched, muttering. But when Jian puts his foot on the line, he finds that it is not there.

The light has gone out. Not dimmed: gone. A stretch of three paces, bare ground and bare water, where for a moment nothing hums at all.

"Pebble."

"It is the seam." The small gray creature has turned on the far bank, and his black eyes are bright. "The road is old. In places it is worn thin. The Keeper must carry himself across."

"Carry myself?"

"You have a Core. Core Step." Pebble tilts his head. "The Interface called it online, on the night of the flowering. I think it is time to learn what that means."

He looks down at his own boots. The panel has said nothing in two weeks. In the corner of his eye, where the little blue lines of the Interface used to sit, there is only one tiny gray line, as faint as a thread, that has been there since the night the stone burned.

```
STANDBY :: Searching. Day 17.
```

He had thought, when it first went quiet, that he would feel it as a loss, a limb gone numb. He had been right. But he had not guessed how clearly he would feel the other thing, in its place: the Core. A round bright weight in the center of his chest, warm and heavy and gold, humming faintly with the road.

It knows, says the boy. Where to go. Can't you feel it?

He can. It is a kind of tug, like a hand on a sleeve. He closes his eyes and breathes out, and lets his weight go forward onto the toes of his left foot, and steps.

It does not feel like a step.

It feels like a held breath being let go. The world slides, a lurch behind the eyes, a cold wind that is not a wind, and then his boot comes down on firm ground a yard past the bare patch, and the line of silver is humming under it. He stands for a moment swaying.

"Excellent," says Pebble. "Four paces. Do it again, but gentler."

"That was not gentle?"

"You nearly went into the river."

* * *

The cost, he finds, is small and clear.

It comes the third time. He has stepped three times across the bare patches of the road, forty paces, sixty, a hundred, and each one a little smoother than the last. On the fourth he sets down on the far side of a ravine, fully twenty paces from where he began, and for a moment the world swims and he has to put out a hand. When he draws it back, the skin on the knuckles is wrinkled.

He looks at his hand. It is the same hand. White-haired and veined, a little spotted, an old man's. But it is, he realizes, a very little older. The cords stand out more sharply under the skin. A faint tremor runs along the third finger.

It's the gold, says the boy.

How do you know?

I can see it. A pause. From the room. The Core is a window. I look through. There's a ring around it, very thin, and every time you step, a little bit of the ring goes dark.

Jian stops walking. He sets down his staff and sits on a flat stone, and Bell looks round, and Yue turns her gray head.

"Wear," he says slowly. "Core wear. Each step shaves a fraction of the gold. It comes back with rest and food and good air, I think. But not all of it."

"How much?" says Bell, sharply. She is already at his side, with two fingers on his wrist. "How many?"

"The boy says a hair per ten steps."

"A hair of what?"

"Of my life." He smiles, a little. "I think, if I stepped every hour for a day, I would be a year older at dusk. If I stepped constantly I would grow old in a week."

Bell's face does something fierce and tight. She digs in her satchel and brings out a flask. "Drink this."

"What is it?"

"Ginseng and honey. Your mother's recipe. It will not heal you, but it will make me feel better." She watches him swallow. "Master Jian. I am a doctor. I would like it on the record that I do not approve."

"So noted."

"Good." She pats his shoulder, hard. "Do not step when you do not have to."

He looks at the line of the road, thin and silver and winding away over the hills, and at the bare gaps in it where the seam has worn thin, and counts. There are, by the look of it, a great many.

We'll manage, says the boy.

I know.

It's a long way.

It is. He gets to his feet. But I would rather walk it with you than anyone.

* * *

They camp that night in a hollow beside the road, out of the wind.

It is a bleak, open place, a shallow dip in the hills with a ring of stunted thorn-bushes and a scatter of black rocks. There is no wood. Bell lights a small oil stove and boils rice, and they sit around it in the blue dusk with their cloaks pulled tight, eating from tin bowls. The silver line runs past the hollow's edge a dozen paces off and glows faintly in the dark, like a river of moonlight.

"Tell me what it is," says Bell, after a while. "The first world. I have heard the word all my life. I have never understood it."

Jian puts down his bowl. He is aware of the boy listening, quietly, in the back of his mind.

"I remember very little," he says. "Fragments. A room with a window. A cold cup of coffee. A word, workstation. I do not know what any of them mean. Ethan Cole wrote that he built a machine to read a man all the way down, memory and habit, and put the whole record on a surface. He put a copy of himself to sleep and sent other copies here." He rubs his face. "That is all I know. A man with a daughter who was afraid."

"And the others? The seven?"

"Children. Who were put in the same cradle, and did not die when the Operator did. Who have been asleep for six hundred years." He looks at the stars. "I do not know what they will be like. I do not know if they will want to wake."

Yue signs, slowly, and Pebble relays. They will want to. Everyone wants to be woken.

"Do they?"

I would have. She smiles. If anyone had held out a hand.

The stove ticks. A cold wind stirs the thorns.

May I say something? says the boy.

Of course.

I'm scared of them. The small voice is almost inaudible. They're like me. They're the same. And they've been alone for six hundred years, and I've had you for eighty-six. What if they hate me?

They will not.

How do you know?

Because you will not let them. Jian shifts his staff across his knees. Because you are the one who answered. Because the first thing any child needs is somebody who says hello.

Silence. Then, very softly, the boy says, I did say hello.

You did.

It was a good hello.

It was the best one I ever heard.

* * *

At the third watch, Yue wakes him by putting a cold hand on his shoulder.

The camp is dark. The stove has gone out. Overhead the stars are huge and hard and brilliant, and the silver road has dimmed to a bare line, and she is sitting upright in her bedroll with her head tilted and her eyes closed. Pebble is on her knee. He too is very still.

What is it? Jian signs, as best he can.

Yue's hands move. Pebble's voice, relaying, is low and strange. The road is humming differently. It was a D. It is a G now. It's coming from the north.

What is?

I don't know. It's very low. It sounds like many feet.

He lies quite still. The Core, in his chest, has gone cold and heavy. The tiny gray line in the corner of his eye is unchanged. The stars wheel overhead, and in the blue dark beyond the hollow the long wall of the mountains stands against the sky like a drawn breath.

The Wall, says the boy.

Yes.

It's breathing, isn't it? In and out.

He does not answer. Beside him Bell stirs and mutters in her sleep. The silver line pulses once, faintly, and fades.

```
STANDBY :: Searching. Day 18.
CORE: wear 0.3%
```

He reads it three times. Then he closes his eyes, and lets go, and goes to sit at the plain round table in the little room with the stove, where a thin dark-eyed boy in a white shirt is waiting with a cup of tea he cannot drink.

"Tell me about the apples," says the boy.

So he does, until morning.

* * *

On the second morning they come to a place where the road has been cut.

It is a gorge, perhaps sixty paces across, with a drop of two hundred feet to a thread of black water. The silver line runs to the edge and stops. On the far side it picks up again, as bright as ever, humming. Between the two there is nothing but air and the wind and the sound of ice cracking in the depths.

Bell looks at the gap. She looks at the sky. She looks at Jian.

"No," she says.

"It is sixty paces."

"You said a hair of your life per ten steps."

"I did not say I would take six steps." He studies the far edge. "I think I can do it in one."

"In one!"

"Core Step is not a stride. It is a fold." He is not sure where the knowledge comes from. It is simply there, in the weight of the gold, a clean small fact like the address of a house. "I do not walk the distance. I move the place where I stand."

That's right, says the boy, with sudden excitement. I can show you. Look.

And in the room behind his eyes, at the round table, the boy lays his two small hands flat on the wood, a hand's breadth apart, and then, with great care, slides the left over the right. Not across the table. Under it. As if the table were a cloth, and he had pinched it, and the two places had touched.

Like that, says the boy. It's not far if you don't make it far.

Jian stands very still. He feels the gold hum. He feels the weight in his chest, and the thread of silver that runs out through his feet into the road, and the long cold gap in it, and he does what the boy does: he does not cross it. He folds it.

The world creases. The wind stops, and the sound of the ice, and for the space of a heartbeat he is standing nowhere at all. Then the line of silver is under his feet, and Bell is shouting from the far side, small and frantic, sixty paces behind.

He checks his hand. It is a little older. But the tremor is faint, and the skin has barely changed.

One hair, says the boy, looking through the Core. Not six. Just one.

Better.

I told you. The boy's voice is bright with pride. You were making it harder than it was.

He laughs aloud, standing alone on the edge of a precipice, in the cold bright morning, with the Sky Wall shining at the end of the world. Then he turns and folds the gap again, back, to fetch the others.

* * *

On the third day they come to the waystation.

It stands on a low hill beside the road, a squat round building of fitted gray stone with a flat roof and a single door. There is no village. There is no sign of a road but the silver one. The building has been there so long that the grass has grown up around it and the stones have gone soft and green with moss, and yet the door, when Pebble nudges it with his nose, swings open easily on silent hinges, and the air inside is dry and sweet.

It is a single room. Six cots with folded blankets. A stove, cold but clean. A table. Shelves of tinned food, sealed in wax, each marked with the same open spiral. On the wall opposite the door, in a frame of black iron, hangs a bronze plaque the size of a tray, engraved with a list of names.

Jian reads it standing, with his hat in his hand.

Operator 2. Operator 3. Operator 4. Operator 5. Operator 6. Operator 7. And beneath them, in a slightly different hand, a line that has been scratched into the bronze with a nail: Operator 8: not yet. Please be kind.

He puts out a hand and touches the scratches. They are shallow and clumsy, and under them runs a thin dark seam of corrosion where the metal has begun, in six hundred years, to heal itself.

"They put this here for you," says Bell, behind him.

"For me. For the one who came last." He feels the boy go quiet. "Seven of them. And every one of them had a child."

There is a second thing on the wall, below the plaque, at the level of a small hand. He crouches. It is a drawing, scratched into the plaster with a stone: seven small stick figures in a row, each holding the hand of the next. The last one has no head. Beside it, in a child's uneven scrawl, are three words.

Come and get us.

Nobody speaks. After a while Yue kneels beside him and lays her palm flat on the drawing. Her eyes are closed. Pebble, on her shoulder, makes a small, low sound, like a kettle going off the boil.

She says, he relays at last, that it was drawn by a boy of eleven. In the fourth year after the last Operator died. He waited here for eleven days.

"Waited?"

For a door that had not yet opened. The voice is very soft. Then he went back, and lay down in his bed, and went to sleep again. Because he thought it was his turn.

Jian rises slowly. He does not trust himself to speak. He walks to the stove, kneels, and with hands that are not quite steady, lights it. The little room fills slowly with warmth. Bell puts a pot on it. Yue sits on a cot with her back against the wall and her eyes closed, listening to something that none of the rest of them can hear.

They stay the night. It is the first time in weeks that he has slept under a roof.

* * *

Later, with the others asleep, he sits by the stove with Bell.

She is awake because she is always awake, he thinks; she has the habit of a doctor, a chronic watchfulness that does not sleep when anyone near her is hurt. She has her satchel open on her knees, and a small notebook, and she is writing in it by the light of the coals.

"What are you counting?" he asks.

"Your hands." She does not look up. "Every morning. I look at the knuckles, the tendons, the skin on the back. I make a note. I have six days of notes now." She taps the page. "The rate is not constant. It depends on what you eat, how you sleep, whether you've stepped. But if I average it, you are aging about a month for every day on the road."

"A month a day."

"Roughly." She lifts her head. Her eyes are sharp and tired. "That is acceptable. If it were a year a day, I would turn us around. I'm telling you so that you know the number. I don't want you to find out later by looking in a glass."

He is silent. Then, to his own surprise, he smiles.

"Thank you."

"For what?"

"For telling me." The coals tick. "Everyone I have ever loved has been trying to protect me from a number. It is very restful to meet someone who hands it to me."

Bell closes the notebook. She is thirty-seven. She has the Lin eyebrows and the Lin chin and, he sees now, her grandmother's way of saying a hard thing in a plain voice. She sets the book aside.

"May I ask you something? Not as a doctor."

"Yes."

"Are you afraid?"

He considers it honestly. The stove ticks. Outside, the wind moves in the thorn-bushes, and on the hill, faintly, the silver road hums.

"Yes," he says. "I am afraid of two things. That they will hate us. And that they will not."

"Not?"

"If they do not hate us, I will have to love them. And I do not think I can bear to lose seven more."

Bell nods slowly. She says nothing. She only reaches across, and takes his hand, and holds it, a warm small practical hand, until the coals go dark.

Goodnight, says the boy, from the room, very softly.

Goodnight.

Brother?

Yes?

I think I'm going to like the first world. A small sleepy pause. Even if it's sad.

He lies back on the narrow cot with the blanket to his chin and listens to the road hum, a long low note, like a lullaby sung by something very old, and the moss-grown stones around him breathe in the dark, and he sleeps.
